about.title: Carson Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Carson is a working city. People here spend their days moving through warehouses near the I-405, shopping centers along Avalon Boulevard and Carson Street, apartment complexes, gas stations, and the campus and event venues that draw visitors from across Los Angeles County. Every one of those places has an owner or operator responsible for keeping walkways reasonably safe. When a spill sits unattended, a handrail comes loose, or a parking lot pothole goes unmarked, the person who falls is often left wondering whether anyone will take responsibility. California premises liability law asks a specific question: did the property owner know about the hazard, or should they have known, and did they fail to fix it or warn about it? Answering that question depends heavily on evidence gathered early, including photographs, incident reports, witness names, and store surveillance footage that is frequently erased within days. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Carson residents with an independent attorney who can evaluate what happened and explain your options.

whyChoose.title: Why Carson Residents Use LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Notice is the heart of the case
items.desc: In California, you generally have to show the owner knew or should have known about the hazard and did nothing. An attorney can look for cleaning logs, prior complaints, and maintenance records that show how long a problem existed.

items.title: Video disappears quickly
items.desc: Most Carson stores, apartment buildings, and parking structures overwrite surveillance footage on a short loop. Getting a preservation letter out early is one of the first things an attorney will want to do.

items.title: Fault is shared, not all-or-nothing
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, so even if the property owner argues you were distracted or wearing the wrong shoes, a claim can still move forward with your share of responsibility factored in rather than ending it outright.

items.question: I fell in a Carson store and the manager wrote up a report. Do I still need to do anything?
items.answer: Yes. The store's report belongs to the store, and you may never see a copy. Take your own photos of the hazard and the surrounding area, write down what you remember while it is fresh, and get names and phone numbers of anyone who saw you fall. If the location had cameras, ask in writing that the footage be saved.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a premises liability claim in California?
items.answer: For most privately owned property, the deadline is two years from the date of the fall. If the property belongs to a public entity, such as a city sidewalk, a county facility, or a public campus, the window is considerably shorter and starts with a formal government claim rather than a lawsuit. Because it can be unclear who owns a given walkway, it helps to have an attorney sort that out early.

items.question: The property owner says the hazard was obvious and I should have seen it. Does that end my case?
items.answer: Not by itself. California uses pure comparative fault, which means a jury or insurer can assign a percentage of responsibility to you and still hold the owner accountable for the rest. An attorney can evaluate whether the hazard was truly visible, whether warnings were posted, and how the lighting and layout affected what a reasonable person would have noticed.
